title: The world's largest single flower grows on a plant with no leaves, stem or roots
body: *Rafflesia arnoldii*, from the rainforests of Sumatra and Borneo, opens a flower about **1 m across**. The rest of the plant has no leaves, stem or roots, and no chlorophyll, so it cannot make its own food. It lives as a parasite hidden inside the tissue of *Tetrastigma* vines, feeding entirely on its host, and can be seen only when a bud breaks out ready to flower. The open bloom smells of rotting flesh, which draws in the flies that pollinate it.

cover.alt: A huge red Rafflesia arnoldii flower with five thick white-spotted petals and a deep central cup, lying on the forest floor

slides.question: How heavy can a single Rafflesia arnoldii flower get?
slides.explanation: Up to about 11 kg. The widest one ever measured was 1.14 m across, and even the buds are typically about 30 cm wide.

slides.heading: A life spent mostly out of sight

steps.label: Its tissue grows hidden inside a vine
A bud forms on the vine's root or stem
The bud swells for many months
The flower opens for just a few days

slides.heading: Why it stinks: to lure flies
slides.text: Chemical studies traced the smell to sulfur compounds such as dimethyl disulfide and dimethyl trisulfide. Each flower is either male or female, so a fly has to visit a male flower first and then a female one for seeds to form.

slides.heading: Rafflesia: true or false?

items.text: Each flower is both male and female
An open flower lasts for months

slides.explanation: The flowers are either male or female, and an open bloom lasts just a few days after a bud that took many months to grow.
